# What Does EDI Capable Mean in a Retailer Letter?


By[Peter Spaulding](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/peter-spaulding) , *Sr. Content Writer*


Last Updated November 19, 2026


8 min read


In this article, learn about:


-


- What the phrase means when no standards body issues the credential


The five things a retailer letter specifies, and where each one sits


How capable, compliant, and certified differ once testing starts


Which path to[EDI capability](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/edi/) fits a smaller supplier


A retailer onboarding letter arrives with a phrase in it that sounds like a certification: your company needs to be EDI capable by a stated date. Searching the phrase returns definition pages, most of which explain electronic data interchange (EDI) in general terms and stop there.


Those pages leave out the part that decides your deadline. No organization issues an EDI capability credential, and the X12 standard governs the format of the files rather than who is permitted to send them.


“Capable” means whatever the retailer that sent your letter says it means, down to the twelve-digit cap one retailer puts on an invoice number. That letter is the only document that answers the question for your account.


## What Does “EDI Capable” Actually Mean?


Being EDI capable means a supplier can exchange the business documents a given retailer requires, in that retailer’s format, over a connection that retailer accepts, and can pass that retailer’s test before its deadline.


The documents are numbered under the X12 standard. A first-time retail supplier usually meets four of them:


-


- **850** (Purchase Order): the order the retailer sends, covering items, quantities, prices, and delivery location


**855** (Purchase Order Acknowledgment): what the supplier can actually fill, including shortages, substitutions, and backorders


**856** (Advance Ship Notice, or ASN): pallet and carton detail, barcodes, and tracking, sent before the truck arrives


**810** (Invoice): the request for payment, which the retailer checks against the 850 and the 856


A fifth document, the **997** functional acknowledgment, is a technical receipt confirming a file arrived and passed formatting checks. It does not confirm the order can be filled.


Capability is not the same as owning EDI software. A supplier can run a well-regarded EDI system and still fail a retailer’s requirements, because the mandatory fields belong to the retailer. Walmart states this directly in its own supplier guidance: transactions have to comply with Walmart’s specifications, which can differ from other retailers’ implementations of the same transaction sets.


**Related Reading:**[EDI for First-Time Suppliers: A Plain-English Guide to the Documents You’ll Send](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/edi-for-first-time-suppliers-a-plain-english-guide-to-the-documents-youll-send)


## What Do Retailer EDI Requirements Actually Specify?


A retailer letter is broken down into five things, though it rarely labels them that way.


What the letter says


What it means for you


“Mandatory transactions”


The numbered documents this retailer requires, a shorter list than the full X12 catalog


“Our specifications”


A separate implementation guide naming the fields, codes, and formats this retailer accepts


“Certification” or “testing”


A period of sending test files until the retailer approves production traffic


“Decision date” and “compliance date”


Two deadlines, usually weeks apart, that the letter may not define


No mention of ownership


The person on your side who answers the retailer’s emails


### Which Documents the Retailer Requires


Dollar Tree Import’s supplier program lists three transaction documents for its vendors: the **810** invoice, the **850** purchase order, and the **860** purchase order change. Walmart publishes specifications for eight, including the **824** (Application Advice) and the **879** (Unit Cost Price Information Advice), though that set covers dropship vendors rather than every Walmart supplier.


### Which Connection the Retailer Accepts


Walmart’s dropship vendor documentation names four connection types: **AS2** , a value-added network (VAN), **SFTP** , and a solution provider that handles EDI processing on the supplier’s behalf. Each one carries its own setup work.


Suppliers sending production files to Walmart over SFTP, for instance, follow a file naming convention down to the second (a document type code, the vendor ID, a GMT timestamp, and a six-digit suffix).


### What EDI Certification Involves


A retailer’s implementation guide is where capability stops being a concept. Dollar Tree Stores publishes a 33-page guide for the **810** invoice alone, specifying segments and elements including **ISA** , **GS** , **BIG** , **N1** , **ITD** , **DTM** , **IT1** , and **TDS** . Several of those elements are mandatory only for Dollar Tree.


The same guide states flat rules that have nothing to do with the standard and everything to do with the retailer’s own systems.


- The payable system accepts invoice numbers no longer than twelve digits


- Purchase order numbers contain no hyphen


- Zero invoices are rejected outright


- Code **FN** is the only value allowed in the **CAD07** element


Test files are marked as such. In the X12 envelope, the **ISA15** element carries a **P** for production or a **T** for test, which is how a retailer’s system tells a practice run from a live document.


### When the Deadline Falls


Dollar Tree Import gives its suppliers a 60-day period to become capable of the electronic requirements, split across three phases: consultation, implementation, and production. Its supplier site references two dates during those phases, a decision date and a compliance date, without defining either one.


### Who Owns It Internally


Retailer programs name their own counterpart and expect yours. In Dollar Tree Import’s program, the retailer confirms a vendor and submits it to SPS, an SPS team member makes contact, and a dedicated analyst stays with the supplier through implementation.


At a smaller supplier that counterpart is frequently the owner, who is also running everything else. Naming the person before the consultation phase is essential for keeping those two dates from arriving unnoticed.


**Related Reading:**[A New Supplier’s Guide to Retailer Compliance Manuals and Deadlines](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/a-new-suppliers-guide-to-retailer-compliance-manuals-and-deadlines)


## EDI Capable, EDI Compliant, EDI Certified: What Is the Difference?


Vendors use these three words inconsistently, and no standards body separates them. What matters is how a retailer’s own program treats a supplier at each stage.


Dollar Tree Import’s program treats capable and certified as different states. A supplier already capable of electronic orders still conducts[certification for the mandatory transactions](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/testing-and-certification/) .


A file can be valid X12 and still fail, because it omits a field that is mandatory only for that retailer. The useful question for the retailer’s onboarding contact is which of the three words appears in its own documentation, and what event marks the end of each stage.


## What Happens If You Miss the Date?


Documentation failures cost money through the remittance rather than through an invoice. Late or inaccurate advance ship notices are among the largest causes of chargebacks, and a missing or late **856** can cause a retailer’s system to reject an entire shipment. A deduction is a penalty taken out of the supplier’s payment, so the revenue loss appears after the goods have shipped.


Smaller rules carry the same weight. Dollar Tree Import’s invoice guide states that a valid Forwarders/Agents Reference (FCR) number is required before an invoice can be processed and payment arranged.


**Related Reading:**[Understanding Retailer Deductions, Chargebacks, and Fines](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/understanding-retailer-deductions-chargebacks-and-fines)


## Which Path Should You Take To Become EDI Capable?


Three arrangements are common in the retail industry:


- Smaller suppliers often use web-based services, where staff enter order data online


- Larger companies usually connect EDI software directly to their own systems


- A value-added network sits between the two companies and moves the files


Some retailers also run a free portal, as Walmart does with WebEDI, which works but takes more manual effort per order. Choosing among providers is a separate exercise with its own comparison criteria.


## What Should You Ask Your Retailer First?


Suppliers who stay on schedule tend to resolve these questions before evaluating any provider:


- Which numbered documents are mandatory for this account, and which are optional


- Where the implementation guide lives, and which version is current


- Which connection types the retailer supports for a supplier of this size


- What test files the retailer expects, and what marks certification as complete


- Which date is the decision date, which is the compliance date, and what happens at each


- Who at the retailer answers questions during implementation


**Related Reading:**[What Happens After a Retailer Says Yes: The First 90 Days for a New Supplier](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-happens-after-a-retailer-says-yes-the-first-90-days-for-a-new-supplier)


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is “EDI capable” an official certification?


No. No standards organization issues it. The X12 standard governs the file format, and each retailer defines capability in its own requirements documentation.


### How long does a retailer usually give a supplier?


It varies. Dollar Tree Import’s supplier site states a 60-day period to become capable of its electronic requirements, and other retailers set their own windows. The letter is the authority for a given account.


### Do all retailers require the same EDI documents?


No. Retailers differ on which documents they require, and they implement the same transaction set differently (Walmart says so in its own supplier guidance), so a supplier already trading with one retailer may still have work to do for the next.


### What happens if we are not capable in time?


That depends on the program. Dollar Tree Import lets a supplier run documents through a service until certification completes. Other retailers treat the compliance date as firm, with order rejections and deductions following.
